title: Scaling Analysis of Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Tokenized Asset Option Pricing: Validation and Barriers to Practical Advantage
abstract_summary: This preprint implements Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) to price European options on tokenized blockchain assets and empirically validates the theoretical O(1/ε) scaling across 3–6 qubit discretizations. Using noise-free simulation the study finds discretization error is the dominant bottleneck at current qubit counts (5–6 qubits), so despite modest NISQ circuit requirements there is no practical advantage today; the author estimates ~3–5 years of hardware improvements (≈7 more qubits and better fidelities) are needed for production-grade accuracy.
methodology_description: The study implements an end-to-end Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) pipeline to price European call options on a tokenized asset (Bitcoin token) in an idealized, noise-free simulation. The terminal price distribution is modeled as log-normal (Black–Scholes assumptions) and discretized into n = 2^q bins spanning [µ ± 3σ]. Bin probabilities are computed via the log-normal / normal CDF (Φ) differences. These probabilities are amplitude-encoded into a quantum state |ψ> over q price qubits. A payoff oracle maps price-bin indices to an objective qubit marking in-the-money (ITM) bins and encodes normalized payoff (Si − K)/(Smax − K). QAE is performed by constructing the Grover/Q operator and applying quantum phase estimation (using m evaluation qubits) to recover the amplitude a = Σ_{Si>K} p_i · ((Si − K)/(Smax − K)); the discounted option price C = e^{-rT} (Smax − K) · a. Experiments sweep price-qubit counts q=3..6 (8–64 bins) to empirically validate scaling; QAE results are compared to the analytical Black–Scholes price and to classical Monte Carlo baselines with varying sample sizes. All quantum experiments are run with a statevector simulator (Qiskit Aer), using 8,192 measurement shots, and report price estimates, absolute errors, and error bars. Circuit resource estimates (total qubits q + m + 1, gate count ≈250, depth ≈150, linear topology) are recorded to assess NISQ feasibility. The methodology isolates algorithmic/discretization effects by using noise-free simulation and excludes state-preparation cost from query-complexity accounting.
experimental_setup: Statevector simulation using Qiskit Aer (noise-free). Shots: 8,192. Backend: CPU (GPU optional). Circuits use q price qubits + m evaluation qubits + 1 objective qubit. Gate count ≈250, circuit depth ≈150, assumed linear nearest-neighbor topology. Experiments sweep q = 3..6 (n = 8..64 bins) with m = 3 evaluation qubits in primary runs (example: q=5, m=3 → 9 total qubits).
dataset_used: Synthetic option pricing data derived from a log-normal terminal price model (Black–Scholes assumptions) for a tokenized Bitcoin asset. Parameters: S0 = $50,000, σ = 80% annual volatility, r = 5% annual risk-free rate, T = 1 year, strike K = $55,000. Continuous log-normal distribution discretized into 2^q bins.

experiment_input.size: Discretizations with n = 2^q bins where q ∈ {3,4,5,6} (n = 8,16,32,64)
experiment_input.preprocessing: Bins cover [µ − 3σ, µ + 3σ] of the log-price; for each bin i compute probability p_i = Φ((ln S_{i+1} − µ)/(σ√T)) − Φ((ln S_i − µ)/(σ√T)). Payoffs per bin computed as max(S_i − K, 0); normalized by (Smax − K) for amplitude mapping. State-preparation routines assumed to prepare amplitude √p_i but their implementation cost is not included in query-complexity accounting.

steps: 1) Specify option and asset parameters (S0, σ, r, T, K).
2) Discretize terminal log-normal price into n = 2^q bins over [µ ± 3σ].
3) Compute bin probabilities p_i via normal CDF differences.
5) Build payoff oracle Of that attaches f(S_i) (ITM indicator and normalized payoff) to an objective qubit.
6) Construct Grover/Q operator Q = −A S_0 A† S_ψ (as per amplitude amplification).
7) Apply Quantum Phase Estimation using m evaluation qubits to estimate rotation angle θ where sin^2(θ) = a.
8) Measure and post-process amplitude a to compute discounted option price C = e^{−rT} (Smax − K) · a.
9) Repeat for qubit counts q = 3..6; collect price estimates, absolute errors, and error bars (via shots).
10) Compare quantum estimates to analytical Black–Scholes price and to classical Monte Carlo runs (varying sample counts e.g., 1k, 10k, 100k, 1M).

key_findings: [supported] Empirical validation (noise-free statevector simulation) that Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) exhibits the predicted O(1/ε) scaling for the tested European option pricing instances, observed as an exact 2.00× error reduction per qubit doubling across 3–6 price qubits (8–64 bins).
[supported] Discretization (binning) error scales as O(1/√nbins) for the log-normal terminal price distribution used, and at low qubit counts dominates total pricing error.

[supported] For the implemented circuits (q price qubits + m evaluation qubits + 1 objective qubit) the example configuration q=5, m=3 requires 9 total qubits, ≈250 gates, and ≈150 circuit depth under a nearest-neighbor linear topology assumption.

[supported] Under idealized, noise-free simulation, the quantum estimate for the BTC-token example produced a point estimate that was within a few percent of Black–Scholes, but with very large discretization-driven uncertainty (example: estimate $14,288 with ±$12,404 error bar, ≈84% relative uncertainty at 5 qubits).
[supported] Classical Monte Carlo baselines reported: 100k samples produce ≈0.23% uncertainty in the test case and far smaller wall-clock times in the simulation environment used.

[supported] Quantitative extrapolation from the discretization curve: roughly 9 qubits are needed to reach ~10% pricing accuracy and ~12 qubits to reach ~1% accuracy for the discretization scheme used.

[speculative] The theoretical complexity advantage of QAE (O(1/ε) query complexity versus classical O(1/ε^2)) holds as a theoretical result and underlies the expected asymptotic sample-efficiency improvement, but practical realization depends on state preparation, discretization, and hardware noise.

[speculative] State preparation costs (preparing the amplitude-encoded log-normal distribution) were excluded from the query-count accounting; the authors note this overhead could be substantial and might negate practical advantage unless improved preparation methods are used.

[speculative] The authors' assessment that the described circuits are 'algorithmically ready' for NISQ devices but that 3–5 years of hardware progress (to reach ~11–12 reliable qubits with sufficient fidelity/coherence) will be required for production-grade accuracy is a forward-looking projection rather than an empirical demonstration.

[supported] The study does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage on the tested problem; instead it demonstrates that the theoretical QAE scaling holds in idealized simulations but that discretization and state-prep limits preclude current practical advantage.

[speculative] The recommendation that efforts should prioritize improved state preparation, hybrid classical-quantum approaches, and error mitigation aligns with recognized algorithmic pathways but was not empirically tested within the paper.

[speculative] The claim that this is the 'first rigorous experimental confirmation' of QAE scaling for option pricing is a literature-positioning statement and may be contested depending on definitions of 'rigorous' and prior work; it is not independently validated within the paper.
results_summary: The preprint reports an end-to-end, noise-free statevector simulation implementation of Quantum Amplitude Estimation for European option pricing on tokenized assets. It empirically confirms the theoretical O(1/ε) scaling of QAE (manifested as an exact 2× error reduction per qubit doubling over 3–6 qubits) and shows discretization error scales as O(1/√nbins). However, discretization is the dominant error at feasible qubit counts: with 5 price qubits the authors observe very large absolute error bars (~$12k, ≈84% relative uncertainty). Circuit resource estimates for the example are ≈9 qubits and ≈250 gates (linear topology), implying near-term hardware could run similar circuits but noise and state-preparation overhead—excluded from the query analysis—prevent practical advantage. Extrapolations indicate roughly 11–12 qubits would be needed to reach ~1% pricing accuracy, leading the authors to conclude that practical advantage remains theoretical/speculative and would require several years of hardware and algorithmic progress.

Discretization errors observed: 3 qubits (8 bins) → $49,616; 4 qubits (16 bins) → $24,808; 5 qubits (32 bins) → $12,404; 6 qubits (64 bins) → $6,202.

Classical Monte Carlo baselines reported: 1,000 samples → 6.15% relative error; 10,000 → 3.49%; 100,000 → 0.23% (error bar $121.75 reported for 100k? table mixing), 1,000,000 → 0.11%.
Circuit resource claim: for q=5 and m=3, total qubits = 9; gate count ≈250; circuit depth ≈150 (linear nearest-neighbor topology).
Estimated qubit requirements to reach production targets via discretization reduction: ~9 qubits for 10% accuracy, ~12 qubits for 1% accuracy, ~15 qubits for 0.1% accuracy.
Projected timeline claim: 12 reliable qubits feasible in ~2027–2029 (3–5 years from the paper's date).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper empirically validates the theoretical asymptotic scaling (O(1/ε)) of QAE in idealized, noise-free simulation, but it does not demonstrate a practical quantum advantage: discretization error, omitted state-preparation costs, and hardware noise mean that for the tested problem and resource counts the quantum approach is not superior to classical Monte Carlo. Thus any advantage remains theoretical/potential pending algorithmic and hardware advances.
limitations: Discretization error is the dominant source of inaccuracy at feasible qubit counts (e.g., ±$12,404 at 5 qubits) and limits practical utility.
State preparation costs are excluded from the complexity analysis and may be substantial (not accounted in query complexity counts).
Experiments are simulation-only in a noise-free setting; no real NISQ device validation was performed.
Accuracy and uncertainty are insufficient for production use: quantum estimates show large error bars compared with classical Monte Carlo at comparable runtimes.
Comparison baseline is basic Monte Carlo; advanced classical variance-reduction techniques (importance sampling, quasi-MC, etc.) were not benchmarked against the quantum approach.
Problem size handled is small (32–64 discrete price levels); method does not scale to the continuous or high-resolution discretizations used in production systems.
Noise model and gate errors on real hardware are not included; a 250-gate circuit at realistic error rates would have reduced fidelity and require significant error mitigation.
State preparation for log-normal distributions may require expensive classical preprocessing (paper claims possible O(2^n) cost), which could negate the quantum advantage.
Simulation framework (statevector) scales exponentially with qubit count, limiting empirical validation to small q; classical simulation time is not representative of real quantum runtime.
The study does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage and is explicitly positioned as a scaling validation rather than a deployable system.

Resource estimates (e.g., 9–10 qubits, ~250 gates) neglect additional overheads such as connectivity constraints, ancillae for efficient arithmetic, and error-correction overhead for reliable, production-grade qubits.
Projected timeline estimates for reaching required qubit counts and fidelities (3–5 years) are speculative and contingent on multiple uncertain engineering advances.
Error mitigation and running on real hardware would likely increase required shots by 10–100×, adding further runtime and resource overhead.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Finds discretization error from low qubit counts (5–6 price qubits) is the dominant bottleneck, so despite favorable asymptotic scaling there is no practical advantage in current NISQ-era regimes.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Provides concrete resource estimates (total qubits, gate count ≤250, depth ≤150, linear topology) and projects ≈3–5 years of hardware improvement (≈8× more qubits and improved fidelities) required for production-grade accuracy.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Compares QAE results to Black–Scholes analytic prices and classical Monte Carlo (1k–1M samples); classical MC is competitive for the small discretizations tested, eroding immediate practical gains.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Notes a methodological limitation: state-preparation costs are assumed/prepared (amplitude encoding) but excluded from query-complexity accounting, which would further increase practical resource needs if included.

contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — Contradicts optimistic claims of immediate quantum speedup for option pricing: noise-free simulations plus discretization analysis show classical Monte Carlo already matches accuracy for tested instances and QAE offers no practical advantage at q≤6.

contradiction:scalability — While validating the theoretical O(1/ε) scaling in idealized experiments, the paper shows that discretization error and omitted state-preparation costs prevent this asymptotic scaling from translating into real-world advantage at current qubit counts and fidelities.
